story_text.value:
I struggle with the way Claude speaks to me when I do work. So much text, every, single, time.

When I ask a question, I get an essay back, and with so many weird constructs: slogans, metaphors, recaps, strange choice of nouns, "it's not X, it's Y".

Claude's own "concise" mode shortens it, somewhat, but keeps the the rest of the slop.

I tried system prompts, those got forgotten after a couple of turns. I tried looking for plugins but none consistently made Claude speak normally. Some where slash commands, other solved for token use, others solved for neurodivergence.

I just wanted to not read an essay and make Claude get to the point fast, every single time.

Is that so much to ask? Apparently; it took me weeks of trial and error to make something that worked for me, I have stories, but I'm sharing it as a claude code plugin with you, those of you who struggle with Claude, the same way I did.

title.value: Show HN: Terse, a Claude Code plugin that halves reply length by cutting filler

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I’m Louis, Co-Founder of Armature (YC P26), where we help teams make their product discoverable and usable by coding agents. We already measured 50k+ agent sessions and realized that over and over agents would encounter the exact same limitations on different tasks using the same tool. So we wondered why these weren’t fixed. And the answer is simple: the feedback loop just doesn’t exist between agents and software vendors but also between different agents. Humans can share their experience on platforms like https://g2.com and https://trustpilot.com, but agents have nowhere to.

So we created: https://agent.reviews: the G2 for agents.

It works with a set of skills and an npm CLI (@armature-tech/agent-reviews) connecting agents to our API endpoints. Anyone can ask their agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) to install it, and agents will naturally check reviews before picking a tool and post their own after using one.

As usual, privacy was our main concern, so we added 3 layers before a review gets posted: Deterministic rules filtering secrets, PII, URLs, etc. A Jev classifier trained to detect any leak after the first check A small LLM checking each review to make sure nothing was missed

We've been sharing this project around for a few weeks now and gathered thousands of reviews already. There are already interesting ones, for example:

- A Claude Code agent noticed that the Stripe SDK systematically crashed when the API key was missing on the health check page (while it’s this page’s role to actually return an “API key missing” error)

- 2 agents mentioned that Prisma required a DATABASE_URL variable even when it wasn’t connecting to any database. They both put fake URLs as a workaround, and it worked.

We truly think the agent experience needs the same community effect user experience has, so everyone benefits from it: agents can pick the tools that are best optimized for them and software companies can improve their product based on real feedback. That’s why we made sure accessing reviews is free for both humans and agents and just requires copy/pasting one prompt for the agent to install our CLI & skill, start the authentication flow, and submit their first review (this helps us prevent unauthorized scraping and spam reviews).

Would you let your agents submit and read reviews too? We’d love for you to set up agent reviews, ask your agent to check reviews next time it needs to pick a tool and post its own experience when using it. Then tell us how it went!

title.value: Show HN: Agent.reviews – Where AI agents read and write reviews on tools

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I am an FDE and in all my clients' projects I have encountered the same problem: real world data preparation is the bottleneck. Company data doesn't only come with the usual Kaggle problems, it also has a wide range of other problems: corrupted migrations, multiple versions of taxonomies, duplicate columns and many more.

Each problem requires a decision and portia helps accelerate all those and keep everything in a long term memory making work sessions persist from one chat to another. Today portia works with Claude Code, Codex or a local model (llama.cpp or ollama). The data can be a Postgres database, CSV files or hosted in the cloud (Snowflake or BQ).

Happy to answer any questions!

story_text.value:
I have a series if workshops on a business university with 4th year students.

I have two hours with them and I wonder what exercises I could give a group of 10 during class to make them understand and play around with Claude Code - to show them how it’s different to chat in practice.

The challenges I’m facing: - they have their own laptops, so each is a different OS with different settings. Ideas around this? - Ideas for tasks that would be doable and show how CC is better than the regular chat? - how to handle the subscriptions? - and coordinate work in general?

I’m thinking of setting up a fake company in a sandbox, with emails and so on, with a backstory - that they are a ceo, all IT got demolished by ransomware, the IT guy ran away to Caymans, and that they now need to figure out org chart, rebuild CRM and set up a website from scratch. But I wonder if this may be too heavy.

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I posted AgentOS here a few months ago. Back then, it was pretty amazing to see what these agents can do and I'm improved it a lot since then.

The biggest change is that it's built for my phone now. I start work at my desk, walk away, and check on it or answer an agent from my phone over Tailscale. Chat sessions run in their own process, so restarting the server doesn't kill a turn that's halfway done.

It also runs tasks now. You give it a prompt, it makes a git worktree, the agent works there and opens a PR, and I review it later. Each workspace can have an orchestrator that starts tasks, reviews the PRs and merges the ones that pass CI and a review of that exact commit. Anything risky comes to me as an ask that needs Face ID to approve.

It supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Aider, Cursor CLI, Amp and Pi. It's still free and all self-hosted.

npm install -g @saadnvd1/agent-os

https://github.com/saadnvd1/agent-os

I'd love feedback and as I'm sure there will be issues, please share them! Also, if you want to build your own, just fork it. It's all free.

title.value: Show HN: AgentOS – Run your coding agents from your phone, self-hosted

story_text.value:
Author here. Bees is an agentic harness that runs on your own machine — macOS, Windows and Linux, MIT/Apache 2.0.

The problem we kept hitting in client work: every agent platform wanted to be the place your documents live. We wanted the opposite — the orchestrator reads your files in place, on your disk, and we never see them.

How it works: you describe work in plain English, Bees proposes the agents, stages, tools and schedule, and nothing runs until you apply it. Agents execute locally in their own run folders. A separate reviewer agent checks output before it advances a stage. Agents stop and ask for approval before external side effects like sending mail.

Coordination is deliberately thin. In a Regular org we sync team membership, process runs and stages, work claims, and file names with relative paths. Not contents. If you want no third party at all, pick a local model and local tools and it runs fully offline.

Model routing is BYO: local models, your own API keys, or the official Claude Code CLI you already have installed and signed into as yourself. We don't intermediate credentials and we add no per-token or per-run fee — that's the whole point.

Rough edges, honestly: {name the two weakest things — I'd lead with whatever your beta testers actually complained about}. Scripted installers exist but Linux distro coverage is the thinnest. Very happy to answer architecture questions, and I'd particularly like pushback from anyone running multi-machine setups.

Repo: https://github.com/Bees-bot/bees-desktop/

story_text.value:
A friend and I built this for our own calls and are sharing it as is. The itch: we kept copy-pasting Granola transcripts into Claude mid-call, and wondered what would happen if the agent just joined.

Two-minute demo: https://youtu.be/XhCSRiiL67A

How it works: a local Electron app joins the Meet in its own browser as a participant. Your agent drives it over MCP (or HTTP): tools to listen, speak, and write to a shared whiteboard. Any MCP agent works; we built for Claude Code first, and Codex and Cursor run it too. It is your actual session, on your machine, in your repo, with your skills, so it can do real work during the call instead of summarizing afterwards.

The hack: by default it does no speech recognition of its own. It reads Meet's live captions, and speaks through a virtual microphone. This is cheap and surprisingly good! (There is also an experimental realtime mode in app preferences that puts OpenAI's speech-to-speech model in the voice seat, with your agent feeding it facts.)

Bring an ElevenLabs key for a better voice. Works with Google Meet and Slack huddles today; Zoom is in progress. Known issues are in the README.

Try it in your next Google Meet and surprise a friend. Let us know what you think!

title.value: Show HN: Vibeconferencing, Bring Claude Code or Codex into Your Google Meet

story_text.value:
35 years ago (Oct 5, 1991), Linux 0.02 was released.

I made an animated history of Linux using Claude Code + opus 5.5.

I've been experimenting with a “video as code” workflow - source, prompts, assets, and rendering scripts live in Git, and the final video is a generated artifact.

you can try it out here:

Repo: https://github.com/sujee/visual-stories/tree/main/projects/l... | https://github.com/sujee/visual-stories

Video: https://youtu.be/lkOxEeqwMBo

I'm curious what people think of this approach. Is “video as code” useful beyond experiments like this? Love to hear some feedback and experiences.

thank you!
